tagline: Gravel crosses sagebrush plateaus, river canyons and a former travelers’ way station.
intro: The Owyhee Uplands Back Country Byway crosses high-desert plateaus and canyons between Jordan Valley, Oregon, and Idaho 78 near Grand View. Mostly gravel and mainly a lane and a half wide, it crosses flat to gently rolling terrain with occasional short grades reaching 12 percent. The Bureau of Land Management identifies it as a National Back Country Byway and highlights its juniper, mahogany and sagebrush landscapes.

Known locally as Mud Flat Road, it provides the primary access to central Owyhee County. Travel through the region once served mining communities: Jordan Valley began as a supply depot after gold was discovered on Jordan Creek in 1863. Cattle ranches developed to supply the miners. At the eastern end of the corridor, the Turmes family settled in 1880 and operated a way station for travelers for many years.

Heading east from Jordan Valley, follow Jordan Creek past irrigated hay meadows, then climb through juniper and mahogany to sagebrush plateaus. The road drops into the North Fork Owyhee canyon, then later passes the Al Perry Bluebird Trail’s roadside nesting boxes. Beyond a 6,133-foot saddle, descend Poison Creek, where willows, aspens and cottonwoods line the watercourse. Cross salt-desert shrubland and pass Turmes Ranch before reaching Idaho 78.

moments.title: North Fork Owyhee River
moments.text: Stunted old-growth junipers grow among boulders and rock outcrops at the rim of the North Fork Owyhee River canyon. The road drops to the North Fork Recreation Site, where a kiosk explains the canyonlands’ wildlife and history. BLM provides camping and picnicking at the recreation site. Vegetation beside desert streams provides shade that helps keep water cool and able to hold oxygen needed by fish. Shrubs and bank-stabilizing sedges support native fish habitat, including that of redband trout, which are most abundant beneath well-developed streamside canopies. The streamside vegetation also helps reduce erosion along these desert waterways.
moments.notice: Stunted old-growth junipers occupy the rocky canyon rim.

moments.title: Al Perry Bluebird Trail
moments.text: White boxes on roadside posts mark the Al Perry Bluebird Trail between Nickel Creek and Pleasant Valley. The project began in 1977 with 25 boxes along the byway. By 1991, 370 boxes offered nesting sites for mountain bluebirds, Idaho’s state bird. Along this part of the drive, juniper woodland gives way to a high rolling plateau of sagebrush and bunchgrass, with pockets of curlleaf mountain mahogany.
moments.notice: White nesting boxes stand on posts beside the road.

moments.title: Turmes Ranch
moments.text: The old stone buildings at Turmes Ranch remain beside the byway. The Turmes family settled here in 1880, planted an orchard and kept a large garden while raising hay and grain. They also ran a way station for travelers for many years. Across the road, a small cemetery on the hill holds members of the family and several other people.
moments.notice: Look for the ranch’s old stone buildings and the cemetery on the hill across the road.
